intro: A cell is the smallest unit that is alive on its own: a thin membrane enclosing a watery cytoplasm, the genetic material (DNA) and ribosomes that make proteins. Every organism is built from one or more cells, and every cell arises from an existing cell. A human body contains about 37 trillion cells of more than 200 kinds.

Cells come in two basic plans. Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) are single cells, mostly 0.1 to 5 µm across, with no nucleus; their DNA lies in a region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi and protists) keep their DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus and divide their interior into other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum and, in plants and algae, chloroplasts. Eukaryotic cells are usually much bigger: if E. coli were the size of a person, a yeast cell would be about the size of an elephant.

Almost all cells are too small to see with the naked eye, so cell biology began with the microscope. Robert Hooke named 'cells' in 1665 after looking at thin slices of cork, and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, with single-lens microscopes magnifying about 270 times, saw swimming microorganisms in 1676. By 1838-1839 Schleiden and Schwann had concluded that plants and animals are made of cells. Light microscopes cannot resolve detail much finer than about 200 nm, so the inner membranes of organelles and the ribosomes were only revealed by electron microscopy from the 1940s and 1950s; today fluorescent dyes, antibodies and fluorescent proteins pick out each structure in living and fixed cells.

structures.name: Plasma membrane
structures.what: The outer boundary of every cell: a double layer of lipids (mostly phospholipids, plus glycolipids and, in eukaryotes, sterols such as cholesterol) carrying many proteins.
structures.does: Lets some ions and molecules through and keeps others out, and is where cells stick to each other, receive signals and anchor the cytoskeleton or the cell wall.
structures.size: Lipid bilayer about 3-4 nm thick (BNID 112585); red blood cell membrane about 7.5 nm (BNID 103948)
structures.see_it: Much too thin to resolve with light, so it appears as the cell outline. Lipophilic styryl dyes such as FM 4-64 stain membranes, and antibodies against membrane proteins (the Human Protein Atlas lists ezrin, syntaxin 4 and beta-catenin among its markers) outline the cell.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Plasma membrane

structures.name: Cell wall
structures.what: A tough layer built just outside the plasma membrane. Plants use cellulose, hemicelluloses and pectin, fungi mainly chitin, bacteria peptidoglycan; animal cells have none.
structures.does: Gives support and shape, protects the cell and lets it withstand osmotic pressure. In plants, small pores (plasmodesmata) cross the wall to link neighbouring cells.
structures.size: Plant walls range from 0.1 to several µm thick; onion about 100 nm (BNID 106007); budding yeast 70 nm (BNID 108266); Staphylococcus aureus about 18 nm (BNID 108268)
structures.see_it: Bacteria are sorted into two wall types by the Gram stain (gram-positive and gram-negative). In plant tissue the walls give the familiar outlined, box-like cells.

structures.name: Nucleus
structures.what: The large membrane-bound compartment that holds almost all of a eukaryotic cell's DNA, packed with histone proteins into chromosomes.
structures.does: Stores and copies the genome and controls which genes are read. Most cells have one; mature mammalian red blood cells have none and some cells, such as osteoclasts, have many.
structures.size: Typically 2-10 µm across (Milo & Phillips); mammalian cultured cells 7.5 µm, range 5-10 µm (BNID 100440); about 10% of a yeast cell's volume
structures.see_it: The DNA dyes DAPI (excited at 358 nm, emits blue at 461 nm when bound to DNA) and Hoechst 33258/33342 (UV-excited, blue) mark nuclei; DAPI works in fixed and live cells but enters live cells less readily. In stained tissue sections nuclei appear as dark ovals.

structures.name: Nuclear envelope and pores
structures.what: Two lipid bilayers wrapped around the nucleus. The outer one is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum; the inner one is lined by a mesh of lamin proteins (the nuclear lamina). Nuclear pore complexes, each built from about 1,000 protein copies of some 35 different nucleoporins, cross both membranes.
structures.does: Separates the nucleoplasm from the cytoplasm. Small molecules diffuse through the pores, while proteins and RNAs are actively carried in and out. The lamina supports the nucleus and anchors chromatin.
structures.size: Nuclear pore complex about 120 nm across in vertebrates (BNID 103695) and 97 nm in yeast (BNID 103696); about 7 pores per um2 in MDCK cells (BNID 110698)
structures.see_it: Antibodies against lamin B1 or the envelope proteins SUN1, SUN2 and LEMD2 draw a crisp rim around the nucleus. The eight-fold symmetric pore complex has been solved in 3D by electron microscopy.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Nuclear membrane
BioNumbers BNID 110698: NPC density on the nuclear envelope (MDCK)

structures.name: Nucleolus
structures.what: The largest body inside the nucleus, not surrounded by a membrane. It forms around the chromosome regions that carry the ribosomal RNA genes and has three zones: fibrillar centre, dense fibrillar component and granular component.
structures.does: Makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits. It falls apart when a cell enters mitosis and reforms afterwards.
structures.size: About 20% of the nuclear volume in budding yeast (BNID 110468)
structures.see_it: Often visible as a dense spot in the nucleus. Electron microscopy resolves its three zones; live dynamics are followed with fluorescent-protein tags and FRAP. Immunofluorescence markers include UBTF (fibrillar centre), fibrillarin and nucleolin (dense fibrillar component) and nucleophosmin (granular component).

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Nucleoli
BioNumbers BNID 110468: Fraction of nucleolus out of nucleus volume (yeast)

structures.name: Ribosomes
structures.what: Particles of RNA and protein with a small and a large subunit; RNA makes up about two thirds of the mass. Bacterial, archaeal and eukaryotic ribosomes differ but share a common core.
structures.does: Read messenger RNA and join amino acids into proteins. They float free in the cytosol or sit on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
structures.size: About 20-30 nm: E. coli 70S ribosome 21-26 nm (BNID 102320, 100121); volume about 3,000-4,000 nm3; about 26,000 per E. coli cell (BNID 117348)
structures.see_it: Below the resolution of light microscopy. They were first seen in the 1950s as dense granules in electron micrographs, their atomic structures came from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, and in cryo-electron tomograms individual ribosomes can be found and counted by template matching.

structures.name: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
structures.what: Flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) whose outer face is studded with ribosomes, continuous with the outer nuclear membrane and concentrated near the nucleus.
structures.does: Makes and folds proteins that will be secreted or placed in membranes. It is especially prominent in cells such as hepatocytes.
structures.see_it: Live cells: ER-Tracker Green or Red (fluorescent glibenclamide), or a fluorescent protein carrying a signal sequence and the KDEL retention signal. Fixed cells: antibodies to calnexin, PDIA3, HSP90B1 or SEC61B. In electron micrographs the ribosome-covered membranes are easy to recognise.

structures.name: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
structures.what: The ribosome-free, mostly tubular part of the ER network, lying more toward the cell periphery.
structures.does: Makes lipids and steroid hormones and helps detoxify compounds; it is abundant in liver and gonad cells.
structures.size: ER tubules 30-100 nm in diameter (Milo & Phillips)
structures.see_it: The same ER dyes and markers label it; the rough and smooth parts are told apart by shape (sheets versus tubules) and, by electron microscopy, by the presence or absence of ribosomes.

structures.name: Golgi apparatus
structures.what: Stacks of linked, flattened membrane sacs, in mammalian cells sitting beside the nucleus near the microtubule organizing centre. Described by Camillo Golgi in 1898.
structures.does: Modifies newly made proteins and lipids (for example by adding sugars), then sorts and packages them for other organelles, the plasma membrane or secretion.
structures.size: Plant Golgi stacks (dictyosomes) 0.03-0.3 µm³ in volume (BNID 105776)
structures.see_it: Fluorescent ceramides (NBD C6-ceramide, BODIPY FL C5-ceramide) collect in the Golgi of live cells, and wheat germ agglutinin conjugates mark the trans-Golgi. Antibodies to golgins (GOLGB1, GOLGA5) or GORASP2 label it in fixed cells, next to the nucleus.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Golgi apparatus
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus

structures.name: Lysosomes
structures.what: Acidic, membrane-bound sacs filled with digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes, discovered by Christian de Duve in 1955.
structures.does: Break down proteins, lipids, sugars and nucleic acids, including material taken up from outside and worn-out parts of the cell delivered by autophagy.
structures.size: 0.1-1.2 µm, typically about 0.5 µm (BNID 106072); interior pH 4.5-5 (BNID 106074); several hundred per cell
structures.see_it: LysoTracker dyes are weak bases that become trapped in acidic compartments of live cells (LysoTracker Red DND-99: excitation/emission 577/590 nm). A fluorescent protein fused to LAMP1 or antibodies to RAB7A label them as scattered puncta.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Vesicles (lysosomes)
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for lysosomes, peroxisomes and yeast vacuoles

structures.name: Peroxisomes
structures.what: Small organelles with a single membrane and a fine granular interior, usually round. They arise from the ER and can also divide.
structures.does: Carry out oxidation reactions that produce hydrogen peroxide and break it down again with the enzyme catalase; they also break down very-long-chain and branched fatty acids.
structures.size: 0.1-1 µm in diameter (BNID 106729)
structures.see_it: Expressing a fluorescent protein tagged with the peroxisomal targeting signal PTS1, or antibody labelling in fixed cells; Human Protein Atlas markers include AGPS and ACBD5. They appear as small dots near the light-microscope resolution limit.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Vesicles
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for lysosomes, peroxisomes and yeast vacuoles

structures.name: Endosomes and vesicles
structures.what: A family of small membrane compartments. Early endosomes receive material taken in at the cell surface; late endosomes (multivesicular bodies) are filled with internal vesicles; recycling endosomes gather near the microtubule organizing centre.
structures.does: Sort what the cell has taken in: some cargo is sent back to the surface, the rest goes on to lysosomes to be digested. Transport vesicles shuttle cargo between the ER, Golgi and plasma membrane.
structures.size: Early endosomes: vesicles 300-400 nm with tubules about 60 nm wide; late endosomes in HeLa cells about 0.76 µm (BNID 104378)
structures.see_it: Identified by their Rab proteins: Rab5 and EEA1 for early, Rab7 and Rab9 for late, Rab11 for recycling endosomes, used as antibodies or fluorescent-protein fusions. Many vesicles are too small to show any internal detail by light microscopy and appear as dots.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Vesicles
BioNumbers BNID 104378: Diameter of late endosome in HeLa cell
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for lysosomes, peroxisomes and yeast vacuoles

structures.name: Mitochondria
structures.what: Organelles with two membranes; the inner one is folded into cristae. They carry a small genome of their own, a remnant of their origin as engulfed bacteria.
structures.does: Produce most of the cell's ATP and also take part in apoptosis, calcium handling and cell-cycle control.
structures.size: Classic shape about 2 µm long and 1 µm wide, but often a branched network spanning tens of um; roughly 10 per yeast cell and 1,000-10,000 per mammalian cell; 383-882 per HeLa cell (BNID 109409)
structures.see_it: Not visible unless stained. MitoTracker dyes accumulate in active mitochondria of live cells (uptake depends on membrane potential; MitoTracker Deep Red FM survives aldehyde fixation). Fluorescent proteins with a mitochondrial leader sequence, or antibodies to import machinery or citrate synthase, also work. At about 200 nm resolution light microscopy cannot show the two membranes or cristae; electron microscopy does.

structures.name: Chloroplasts
structures.what: Green plastids rich in chlorophyll, with internal membrane sacs (thylakoids) stacked into grana. Like mitochondria they keep their own DNA, a sign of descent from an engulfed cyanobacterium.
structures.does: Carry out photosynthesis: they capture light energy, split water to release oxygen and fix CO2 into sugars, which can be stored as starch granules.
structures.size: About 4-6 µm across, mean volume about 20 µm³; about 100 per leaf mesophyll cell (80-120 in Arabidopsis, BNID 109053); 40-60 grana stacks each
structures.see_it: Seen as green bodies in light micrographs of leaf and moss cells; the grana inside are only just visible with a light microscope. Electron microscopy shows the thylakoid stacks and starch granules.

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are chloroplasts?
BioNumbers BNID 109053: Number of chloroplasts per mesophyll cell (Arabidopsis)

structures.name: Vacuole
structures.what: A membrane-bound, water-filled compartment formed by fused vesicles. Mature plant cells usually have one large central vacuole bounded by a membrane called the tonoplast.
structures.does: In plants it keeps the cell turgid, stores nutrients and breaks down waste; in yeast it plays a lysosome-like role.
structures.size: Usually over 30% and up to 80% of a mature plant cell's volume; 3-14% of a budding yeast cell depending on strain (BNID 111977)
structures.see_it: Because the plant vacuole fills most of the cell, the cytoplasm and chloroplasts are seen squeezed against the cell wall. In yeast, FM 4-64 stains the vacuole membrane red and CMAC-based dyes fill its lumen; acidotropic probes also stain plant vacuoles.

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are chloroplasts?
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for lysosomes, peroxisomes and yeast vacuoles

structures.name: Actin filaments (microfilaments)
structures.what: The thinnest cytoskeletal fibres: two intertwined strands of actin subunits forming a polar filament.
structures.does: Drive cell crawling and shape change, pinch the cell in two during cytokinesis, take part in endocytosis and exocytosis, and, with myosin motors, power muscle contraction.
structures.size: About 7 nm in diameter; each subunit roughly 5 nm
structures.see_it: Fluorescent phalloidin, a mushroom toxin that binds F-actin tightly, is the standard stain for F-actin in fixed and permeabilized cells. Antibodies to vinculin or zyxin mark the focal adhesions where filaments end.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Actin filaments
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are the cell's filaments?
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for actin

structures.name: Microtubules
structures.what: Hollow tubes, usually of 13 protofilaments of alpha/beta-tubulin, radiating from microtubule organizing centres such as the centrosome.
structures.does: Act as tracks for motor proteins carrying vesicles and organelles, build the mitotic spindle that separates chromosomes, and form the core of cilia and flagella.
structures.size: About 25 nm outer diameter (BNID 106123), 11-15 nm inner diameter, up to about 50 µm long
structures.see_it: Anti-alpha-tubulin antibodies in fixed cells or GFP-tubulin in live cells; the drug paclitaxel stabilises microtubules and blocks cells in mitosis.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Microtubules
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for tubulin and other cytoskeletal proteins

structures.name: Intermediate filaments
structures.what: Rope-like, non-polar filaments built from a large family of proteins (about 70 human genes), including keratins, vimentin, desmin, neurofilaments and the nuclear lamins.
structures.does: Give cells and tissues mechanical strength; the lamins form the nuclear lamina.
structures.size: About 10 nm in diameter (8-10 nm, BNID 106125)
structures.see_it: Antibodies to the type expressed in each cell, for example keratins (KRT19, KRT17) in epithelial cells, desmin in muscle and vimentin in fibroblasts and leukocytes, so the stain also hints at the cell type.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Intermediate filaments
BioNumbers BNID 106125: Diameter of intermediate filaments

structures.name: Centrosome and centrioles
structures.what: A non-membrane organelle made of two centrioles set at right angles, each a cartwheel of nine microtubule triplets, surrounded by pericentriolar material containing gamma-tubulin and pericentrin. Plants and fungi lack it.
structures.does: The main microtubule organizing centre of animal cells. In mitosis the spindle forms between the two centrosomes; in many differentiating cells the centrosome gives way to a cilium.
structures.size: Centriole about 0.5 µm long and 0.2 µm wide (BNID 105741); gamma-tubulin ring complex about 25 nm
structures.see_it: Immunofluorescence for centrosomal proteins such as CEP350, ODF2 or PIBF1. Counting centrioles by fluorescence is imprecise because the pair is close to the resolution limit.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Centrosome
BioNumbers BNID 105741: Size of canonical centriole

structures.name: Cilia and flagella
structures.what: Hair-like projections from the cell surface. In eukaryotes the core (axoneme) is nine microtubule doublets around a central pair (9+2) in motile cilia, and without the pair (9+0) in most primary cilia. Bacterial and archaeal flagella are a different, rotating protein machine.
structures.does: Motile cilia and flagella move the cell or move fluid past it; most vertebrate cells carry one non-motile primary cilium that acts as a sensory antenna.
structures.size: Eukaryotic flagellum about 200 nm wide (BNID 104823); bacterial flagellum about 20 nm (BNID 109343); a Paramecium carries about 10,000 beating cilia (BNID 110791)
structures.see_it: Tubulin antibodies stain the axoneme, including primary cilia. At about 20 nm wide, a single bacterial flagellum is far below the roughly 200 nm resolution of fluorescence microscopy, but some large bacteria twist 30 or more into a fascicle that is easily seen with a light microscope.

sources.title: Human Protein Atlas, subcellular section: Microtubules
BioNumbers BNID 110791: Number of beating cilia (Paramecium)

structures.name: Nucleoid
structures.what: The region of a prokaryotic cell that holds the chromosome, usually one circular DNA molecule, packed without a surrounding membrane.
structures.does: Stores and expresses the genome while keeping a very long DNA molecule compact; the E. coli chromosome (about 4.6 million base pairs) would be about 1.5 mm long if stretched out.
structures.see_it: DNA stains such as DAPI show it in fluorescence, the Feulgen stain in bright field, and electron micrographs show it as an irregular region distinct from the cytosol. Overlaying a phase-contrast image of the cell with the DNA fluorescence shows where it sits.

structures.name: Plasmids
structures.what: Small extra DNA molecules, usually circular, that copy themselves independently of the chromosome.
structures.does: Carry optional genes such as antibiotic resistance and can pass between bacteria by conjugation. Engineered plasmids are the everyday tool for putting genes, including fluorescent-protein fusions, into cells.
structures.size: A 10 kbp plasmid has a contour length of about 3 µm (a circle about 1 µm across if laid flat); the yeast 2-micron plasmid is present at 30-40 copies per cell
structures.see_it: Not seen as a distinct structure in routine light microscopy; it is usually studied through the genes it carries.

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are biochemical nuts and bolts?

cell_types.name: Bacterium (E. coli)
cell_types.summary: Bacteria are single cells without a nucleus; their DNA lies in a nucleoid in the cytoplasm. Escherichia coli, a gram-negative rod from the gut, is the standard model bacterium and a handy ruler for the micrometre scale.
features: Short rod about 1 µm wide and 2 µm long
No nucleus: DNA stains (DAPI) show a compact nucleoid
Stains gram-negative (thin peptidoglycan wall plus an outer membrane)
Flagella spread over the whole surface (peritrichous)
cell_types.size: About 1 µm diameter, 2 µm long, volume about 1 µm³ (BNID 100002; Milo & Phillips)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is an E. coli cell and what is its mass?

cell_types.name: Cyanobacterium
cell_types.summary: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria that release oxygen, using chlorophyll, carotenoids and phycobilin pigments held on internal thylakoid membranes. An ancient cyanobacterium engulfed by a eukaryote is thought to be the ancestor of chloroplasts.
features: Blue-green colour from their pigments
Unicellular forms, colonies, or chains of cells (filaments)
Some filamentous species form heterocysts
Photosynthetic pigments held on internal thylakoid membranes
cell_types.size: Synechococcus 0.6-2.1 µm (BNID 108790); Prochlorococcus, the most abundant, about 0.6 µm (BNID 101520)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are chloroplasts?

cell_types.name: Archaeon
cell_types.summary: Archaea are the second domain of prokaryotes: they lack a nucleus like bacteria but differ in their biochemistry, and many live in extreme habitats. Under the microscope most look much like bacteria.
features: Spheres, rods, spirals or plates, much like bacteria
Some unusual shapes, such as the flat square cells of Haloquadratum
No nucleus
Cell walls vary: protein S-layers, pseudopeptidoglycan or polysaccharides
cell_types.size: Commonly 0.5-2 µm (BNID 103059); extremes from about 0.2 µm (BNID 110071) to 15 µm (BNID 110070)

cell_types.name: Budding yeast
cell_types.summary: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, baker's and brewer's yeast, is a single-celled fungus and the model eukaryote, with a nucleus and the usual organelles inside a cell wall. It divides by budding a smaller daughter off a larger mother.
features: Round to oval cells, often with a bud attached
Rigid cell wall
Vacuole, one of the largest organelles, outlined in red by FM 4-64
Haploid cells smaller than diploid cells
cell_types.size: About 4 µm diameter (haploid) and 6 µm (diploid); median volume 42 µm³ (haploid) and 82 µm³ (diploid)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a budding yeast cell?
Molecular Probes Handbook (Thermo Fisher): Probes for lysosomes, peroxisomes and yeast vacuoles

cell_types.name: Diatom
cell_types.summary: Diatoms are single-celled algae found in oceans, fresh water and soils, and a major source of the planet's oxygen. Each cell lives inside an ornate, porous silica shell called a frustule.
features: Glassy silica frustule with regular patterns of pores
Radially symmetric (centric) or, more often, bilaterally symmetric (pennate) shells
Yellowish-brown chloroplasts
Usually no flagella
cell_types.size: Mostly 20-200 µm, overall 2-2000 µm

cell_types.name: Ciliate (Paramecium)
cell_types.summary: Ciliates are protists covered in many short cilia that they use to swim, crawl and feed. Unusually, each cell has two kinds of nucleus: a small germline micronucleus and a large macronucleus that runs the cell.
features: Body covered in beating cilia (about 10,000 on Paramecium caudatum)
Large macronucleus plus a small micronucleus
Common in ponds, lakes, rivers, oceans and wet soil
Paramecium cells are 100-300 µm long
cell_types.size: Species range from about 10 µm to 4 mm; Paramecium 100-300 µm long (BNID 112283)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 112283: Length and number of cilia (Paramecium)
BioNumbers BNID 110791: Number of beating cilia (Paramecium caudatum)

cell_types.name: Amoeba
cell_types.summary: An amoeba is a cell that constantly changes shape by pushing out pseudopods, bulges of cytoplasm driven by actin filaments, to crawl and to engulf food. Amoeboid cells appear in many unrelated lineages.
features: No fixed shape; outline changes as you watch
Pseudopods: blunt lobes in Amoeba, thread-like or net-like in other groups
Freshwater amoebae have a contractile vacuole that pumps out water
Nucleus only about 1.5% of the cell volume in Amoeba proteus
cell_types.size: Amoeba proteus about 0.5 mm3 in volume (BNID 113819); Dictyostelium about 12 µm long (BNID 106826)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 113819: Average cellular and nuclear volume (Amoeba proteus)

cell_types.name: Plant cell
cell_types.summary: Plant cells are eukaryotic cells enclosed in a cellulose wall, with chloroplasts in green tissues and usually a large central vacuole. Cells connect to their neighbours through pores in the wall called plasmodesmata.
features: Outline fixed by the rigid cellulose wall
Large central vacuole pushing cytoplasm to the edge
Green chloroplasts in leaf cells (about 100 per mesophyll cell)
No centrioles (except in some gametes)
cell_types.size: Typically 10-100 µm (BNID 108685)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are chloroplasts?

cell_types.name: Guard cell
cell_types.summary: Guard cells are bean-shaped cells that sit in pairs in the leaf surface, with the stomatal pore between them. By swelling or shrinking they open and close the pore, balancing CO2 uptake against water loss.
features: Paired, bean-shaped cells around a pore
Inner wall facing the pore is thicker
Contain chloroplasts (16 per guard cell in coffee)
Pore wide open when cells are turgid, closed when flaccid
cell_types.size: About 20 µm long and 9 µm wide in Arabidopsis (BNID 107834)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 107834: Dimensions of guard cells (Arabidopsis)
BioNumbers BNID 107031: Number of chloroplasts per guard cell

cell_types.name: Pollen grain
cell_types.summary: A pollen grain is a highly reduced male gametophyte of a seed plant, which produces the sperm cells. Its tough outer wall (exine) is patterned in ways characteristic of each species and survives as fossils.
features: Hard outer wall (exine) made of sporopollenin
Shape and surface markings identify the species
Wings in pine, fir and spruce pollen
Grows a pollen tube on reaching a flower
cell_types.size: From 2.5-5 µm (forget-me-not) to about 90-100 µm (corn); most grass pollen 20-25 µm

cell_types.name: Red blood cell (erythrocyte)
cell_types.summary: Red blood cells carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin and are the most numerous cells in the human body. Mammalian red cells lose their nucleus and organelles as they mature, leaving a flexible biconcave disc.
features: Biconcave disc, thinner in the middle than at the rim
No nucleus or organelles in mammals
About 7-8 µm: a lymphocyte nucleus is roughly the same size
Very flexible, squeezing through narrow capillaries
cell_types.size: Diameter 7.8 µm (BNID 100509), volume about 90-100 µm³ (BNID 115152)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How many cells are there in an organism?

cell_types.name: Neutrophil
cell_types.summary: Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells in humans and usually the first immune cells a pathogen meets. They are granulocytes whose nucleus is split into several lobes.
features: Nucleus with 2-5 lobes (polymorphonuclear)
Cytoplasm stains a neutral pink and holds about 200 granules
12-15 µm across when spread on a blood smear
40-70% of white blood cells
cell_types.size: About 8.4 µm in suspension (BNID 100510); 12-15 µm when spread on a smear

cell_types.name: Lymphocyte
cell_types.summary: Lymphocytes (T cells, B cells and NK cells) are the white blood cells of adaptive immunity and of cell killing. A resting lymphocyte is little more than a large round nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm.
features: Large, dark, dense round nucleus about the size of a red cell
Only a thin rim of pale cytoplasm
Sometimes a clear halo around the nucleus
Smallest common white cell
cell_types.size: About 7 µm diameter (BNID 100507)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 100507: Diameter of peripheral blood lymphocytes
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are nuclei?

cell_types.name: Macrophage
cell_types.summary: Macrophages are large phagocytic cells of the tissues that engulf microbes and debris and signal to other immune cells; they form the mononuclear phagocyte system. In tissue they take local names such as Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages and microglia.
features: Large cell with a nucleus that is small relative to the cell
Phagosomes holding engulfed microbes (3-6 µm in mouse, BNID 116148)
One unlobed nucleus (a mononuclear phagocyte)
Identified with markers such as CD68 or CD14
cell_types.size: Human alveolar macrophage about 21 µm (BNID 103565)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 103565: Diameter of alveolar macrophage (human)
BioNumbers BNID 116148: Diameter of phagosomes containing bacteria (mouse)
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are nuclei?

cell_types.name: Eosinophil
cell_types.summary: Eosinophils are granulocytes that fight multicellular parasites and take part in allergy and asthma. Their granules stain bright red with the acidic dye eosin.
features: Two-lobed nucleus
Granules that stain bright red with eosin
1-3% of white blood cells
12-17 µm across
cell_types.size: 12-17 µm; cell volume about 206 µm³ (BNID 115183)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 115183: Volume of eosinophil cell and nucleus

cell_types.name: Platelet
cell_types.summary: Platelets are not whole cells but fragments of cytoplasm shed by giant megakaryocytes in the bone marrow. They help blood clot, releasing clotting factors and signalling molecules from their granules.
features: Tiny lens-shaped discs, much smaller than red cells
No nucleus
Fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm
Alpha granules (clotting factors) and dense bodies (ADP, calcium, serotonin)
cell_types.size: 2-3 µm across; parent megakaryocytes reach about 100 µm (BNID 106130)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?

cell_types.name: Neuron
cell_types.summary: Neurons carry electrical signals: they receive input mainly through branched dendrites and the cell body (soma) and send output along a single axon to synapses. An adult human brain holds about 86 billion of them.
features: Compact cell body (soma), often not much larger than its nucleus
Branching dendrites reaching a few hundred um
One long axon leaving from the axon hillock
Nissl bodies seen with basophilic dyes; Golgi silver staining picks out a few whole neurons in full detail
cell_types.size: Soma usually 10-25 µm (range 4-100 µm); axons up to about 1 m long in humans (BNID 104901)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 104901: Length of neuron from spine to toe
BioNumbers BNID 106322: Number of neurons in adult male brain
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?

cell_types.name: Glial cell
cell_types.summary: Glia are the non-signalling cells of the nervous system: they support and protect neurons, keep the environment stable and make myelin. They include astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and ependymal cells in the brain and spinal cord, and Schwann and satellite cells in peripheral nerves.
features: Oligodendrocytes (45-75% of brain glia) and Schwann cells wrap axons in myelin
Astrocytes are 19-40% of brain glia
Microglia are small brain macrophages with oblong nuclei, whose processes constantly sample their surroundings
Together glia make up more than half the volume of neural tissue

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 115169: Glial cell density in grey matter

cell_types.name: Skeletal muscle fibre
cell_types.summary: A skeletal muscle cell (fibre) forms when many precursor myoblasts fuse, so one very long cell contains many nuclei. Its contractile units, the sarcomeres, are lined up in register, giving the striped look.
features: Very long fibres
Cross-striations (bands) from aligned sarcomeres
Many nuclei, pressed against the cell membrane at the edge
Much larger than the other cells in the tissue
cell_types.size: Typically about 100 µm in diameter and 2-3 cm long

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?

cell_types.name: Cardiac muscle cell
cell_types.summary: Heart muscle cells are striated like skeletal muscle but are much shorter cells with one or two central nuclei. They are joined end to end by intercalated discs that pass the electrical signal so the heart contracts in a coordinated way.
features: Striated (light I bands, dark A bands)
One, sometimes two, central nuclei
Intercalated discs where cells join end to end
Packed with mitochondria (about 29-36% of cell volume)
cell_types.size: Roughly rectangular, 100-150 µm by 30-40 µm; rat cardiomyocyte volume about 15,600 µm³ (BNID 108243)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 116935: Fraction of cardiac myocyte volume occupied by mitochondria

cell_types.name: Smooth muscle cell
cell_types.summary: Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow organs such as the stomach, intestines, bladder and uterus, and lines most blood vessels; it is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. It has no sarcomeres, so it shows no stripes.
features: Spindle-shaped: wide in the middle, tapering at both ends
A single central nucleus
No striations
Actin filaments anchor to dense bodies instead of Z-discs
cell_types.size: 30-200 µm long when relaxed

cell_types.name: Squamous epithelial cell
cell_types.summary: Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of very flat cells fitted together like paving stones. Its thinness suits diffusion and filtration, so it lines lung alveoli, blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities.
features: Very flat, polygonal cells forming a mosaic
Flattened, oval nucleus in the middle of each cell
Single cell layer
Also called pavement or tessellated epithelium

cell_types.name: Columnar epithelial cell
cell_types.summary: Columnar epithelial cells are tall and narrow, standing side by side on a basement membrane. They line the stomach, intestines and uterus; some carry cilia, others absorb nutrients.
features: Tall, slender cells in a single row
Oval nuclei lined up near the base
Absorptive cells have a brush border of microvilli on top
Ciliated forms move mucus along airways

cell_types.name: Keratinocyte
cell_types.summary: Keratinocytes make up about 90% of the cells of the epidermis, the outer skin. Born from stem cells at the base, they move up while filling with keratin, die as flat corneocytes and are shed.
features: Layered epidermis: dividing basal cells at the bottom, dead cornified cells shed from the top
Basal cells anchored to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes
Rich in keratin intermediate filaments
Turn over every 40-56 days in humans
cell_types.size: Neonatal human keratinocytes about 12.5 µm in diameter in culture (BNID 108894)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 108894: Diameter of epidermal keratinocytes (HEKn)

cell_types.name: Fibroblast
cell_types.summary: Fibroblasts are the most common cells of connective tissue: they secrete collagen and the rest of the extracellular matrix and are central to wound healing.
features: Spindle-shaped or branched cytoplasm
Elliptical, speckled nucleus with two or more nucleoli
Do not form flat sheets like epithelia; inactive fibrocytes are smaller
Vimentin intermediate filaments
cell_types.size: NIH/3T3 fibroblast about 18 µm across (BNID 108905); nucleus about 10 µm

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 108905: Diameter of NIH/3T3 embryonic fibroblast
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are nuclei?

cell_types.name: Adipocyte (fat cell)
cell_types.summary: Adipocytes store energy as fat. A white fat cell is almost entirely one large lipid droplet, with the cytoplasm and nucleus squeezed into a thin rim; brown fat cells hold many smaller droplets.
features: One huge lipid droplet (unilocular) in white fat
Flattened nucleus pushed to the edge
Fat stored in a semi-liquid state, mainly triglycerides
Brown fat: many small droplets (multilocular)
cell_types.size: Estimates vary with method: 30-50 µm (BNID 107466) to a typical 0.1 mm

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 107466: Diameter of adipocyte cell
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How many cells are there in an organism?

cell_types.name: Chondrocyte
cell_types.summary: Chondrocytes are the only cells in healthy cartilage. They make and maintain the cartilage matrix of collagen and proteoglycans in which they are embedded.
features: Rounded or polygonal cells
Sit in the cartilage matrix they secrete
Develop from matrix-secreting chondroblasts
Usually inactive once mature

cell_types.name: Osteocyte
cell_types.summary: Osteocytes are the most common cells in mature bone: bone-forming osteoblasts that became trapped in the matrix they made. They live in small cavities (lacunae) and talk to each other through long processes running in tiny canals (canaliculi).
features: Star-shaped cell in a lacuna
40-60 thin processes running through canaliculi
Single nucleus
Do not divide; can live for decades
cell_types.size: About 7 µm wide and 15 µm long; about 42 billion in an adult skeleton (BNID 111547)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 111547: Total number of osteocytes in the adult skeleton

cell_types.name: Hepatocyte
cell_types.summary: Hepatocytes are the main cells of the liver, making up about 80% of its mass. Rough ER is especially prominent in hepatocytes, and the liver is rich in smooth ER.
features: Large, roughly cube-shaped cells
Round nuclei with dispersed chromatin and prominent nucleoli
Binucleate cells and polyploid nuclei are common
Pale unstained areas where glycogen and lipid were removed in processing
cell_types.size: Sides 20-30 µm; rat hepatocyte volume about 7,000 µm³ (BNID 104616)

cell_types.name: Sperm cell
cell_types.summary: Sperm are the small, motile male gametes. A human sperm delivers a haploid nucleus and the centrioles to the egg, swimming with a single flagellum powered by mitochondria in its midpiece.
features: Disc-shaped head holding densely coiled chromatin, capped by the acrosome
Midpiece packed with mitochondria
One long tail (flagellum) about 50 µm
Swims about 1-3 mm per minute
cell_types.size: Head about 5.1 x 3.1 µm; tail about 50 µm; volume about 28.5 µm³ (BNID 109891)

sources.title: BioNumbers BNID 109891: Isosmotic volume of sperm (human)
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?

cell_types.name: Oocyte (egg cell)
cell_types.summary: The oocyte is the female gamete and one of the largest human cells. It is stocked with cytoplasm and yolk granules to support early development and is wrapped in a glycoprotein coat, the zona pellucida.
features: Very large, round cell
Zona pellucida surrounding the membrane
Cortical granules (0.2-0.6 µm) under the surface
Surrounded by follicle cells in the ovary
cell_types.size: About 120 µm in diameter (BNID 102187)

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?

cell_types.name: Dividing cell (mitosis)
cell_types.summary: In mitosis a eukaryotic cell separates its duplicated chromosomes into two identical nuclei. The stages (prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) are recognised by how the condensed chromosomes and the spindle look.
features: Chromosomes condense and become visible; the nucleolus disappears
Metaphase: chromosomes lined up at the cell's middle on the spindle
Anaphase/telophase: two chromosome sets pulled apart, then a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two
Animal cells round up and the nuclear envelope breaks down
cell_types.size: Mitosis takes about 1 h of a roughly 20 h HeLa cell cycle

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How long do the different stages of the cell cycle take?
Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big are the cell's filaments?

cell_types.name: Cultured cell line (HeLa)
cell_types.summary: Cell lines are cells that keep dividing in the lab, most growing attached to a dish as a single-cell-thick layer. HeLa, the oldest human line, came from the cervical cancer of Henrietta Lacks in 1951, taken without her knowledge or consent.
features: Adherent cells spread flat on the dish, like a fried egg with the nucleus as the yolk
Only a few µm tall but tens of µm across
Pack closer together as the dish fills (confluence)
Rounded when floating or dividing
cell_types.size: HeLa volume about 2,000 µm³ (range 500-4,000); spread about 40 µm across, about 20 µm when confluent

sources.title: Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo & Phillips): How big is a human cell?
BioNumbers BNID 105879: Volume of HeLa cell

cell_types.name: Cancer cell
cell_types.summary: Cancer cells grow and divide without the normal controls. Pathologists recognise them largely by the appearance of the nucleus, which is used in diagnosis and staging.
features: Large, irregularly outlined nucleus
Nuclear grooves, folds or indentations
Clumped or dispersed chromatin and an enlarged nucleolus
Abnormal cytoplasm
